body: Visiting the Nine Arches Bridge was one of the highlights of my trip to Ella. Tucked between lush green hills and surrounded by tea plantations, this colonial era railway bridge feels like something out of a storybook. It's not just a photo opportunity it’s a place where history, engineering, and nature come together beautifully.The walk to the bridge is half the experience. Depending on where you start (from Ella town or from the small road near the Art Café Umbrella), the trail takes about 20–30 minutes. The path winds through quiet jungle trails, small home gardens, and tea fields. It’s a peaceful walk and not very difficult just wear proper shoes if it has rained, as it can get muddy.When you finally reach the bridge, the first view is breathtaking. The Nine Arches, built entirely out of brick and stone without any steel, stretch out across a deep gorge. Trains still run across it a few times a day and if you can time your visit to see one passing over, it’s a magical moment.We arrived just before a train was scheduled and sat with some locals and travelers on the hillside. Everyone fell quiet when the train appeared — slowly curving across the bridge with its horn echoing through the valley. It felt timeless, almost like stepping into a slower, simpler world.Tips:Best time to visit: Early morning or just before sunset fewer crowds and better light for photos.Train times: Ask a local or your guesthouse; trains aren’t always on schedule.For photos: Walk up the little hill opposite the bridge for a great angle with the forest in the background.There are cafés nearby if you want to enjoy a tea or juice with a view.Be respectful it's still an active railway and also a quiet area for locals.Nine Arches Bridge isn’t a long visit maybe an hour or two but it leaves a lasting impression. It’s a peaceful, scenic break from busier tourist sites, and it connects you to the charm of Sri Lanka’s hill country in the most beautiful way.

body: The Nine Arches Bridge, nestled in the scenic town of Ella in Sri Lanka, is a remarkable feat of engineering and a symbol of the island’s natural beauty and colonial past. Completed in 1921 during British rule, this iconic railway bridge spans 91 meters in height and stretches over 300 meters in length, arching gracefully across a lush, verdant valley. Its structure, characterized by nine large arches, is an awe-inspiring example of early 20th-century engineering, built using solid bricks and concrete without the use of steel. The bridge is strategically placed within a landscape of dense forests, rolling hills, and tea plantations, which offers visitors breathtaking panoramic views that have made it one of Sri Lanka's most photographed landmarks.As a key part of the railway line that connects Colombo to Badulla, the Nine Arches Bridge serves not only as a transportation route but also as a historical relic. The surrounding area, rich in biodiversity and serene beauty, has made it a prime destination for nature lovers, adventurers, and photographers. The bridge is often seen as a peaceful contrast to the hustle and bustle of urban life, offering a glimpse into Sri Lanka's colonial heritage.Tourists flock to this bridge to marvel at its intricate design and its ability to blend harmoniously with the surrounding natural environment. Whether visited during the misty mornings or the golden hours of sunset, the Nine Arches Bridge never fails to leave a lasting impression on those who encounter it. It remains an enduring symbol of Sri Lanka’s cultural and natural heritage, standing as a testament to the resilience of both the human spirit and the land it inhabits.

body: How many stone arch bridges (namely stone, without the use of reinforced concrete and other iron) do you know? Until I wrote this post, I didn’t really bother with this issue. It turns out that there are more than enough of them - STONE bridges in the world. True, there are not so many bridges made of stone, whose arched spans are at least 50 meters. Surely you have heard of the Juxigou Bridge in China, the Maidenhead Viaduct in England, the Solkan Bridge in Slovenia, the Heather Bridge in Iran, the Wiesen Viaduct in Switzerland, the Pont de Vieille Briude in France, etc.In total, I managed to count about six dozen wide-span bridges around the world. In reality, there are many times more stone bridges with narrow spans. But they are no less interesting, take the word of an old travel lover!!! But!!! How many of these STONE bridges are railway bridges?Even clever Wikipedia couldn’t answer this for me. During my trip to Sri Lanka, I was able to get acquainted with the local must see, which represents one of the best examples of colonial-era railway construction in Ceylon. Moreover, as they say, “three in one”: this is a BRIDGE, it is STONE and it is RAILWAY!!! I'm talking about the Nine Arches Bridge - the Bridge of Nine Arches. It is built across a swampy lowland near the village of Gotuwala between two railway stations - Ella and Demodara.This bridge is one of the favorite places for party-juice of insta-people: 9 out of 10 travel lovers will definitely not fail to visit this object to photograph the architectural ingenuity of the creators of the Bridge and the abundant tropical greenery on the nearby hillsides, and then post their smiling photo in the virtual world. For lovers of historical and engineering precision, the Nine Arches Bridge is a pain in the ass: only its dimensions are known from accurate information (length - 91.44 meters, width - 7.62 meters, height - 24.38 meters). AND THAT'S ALL!!! As for the time of its construction: according to one piece of information, work on the construction of the bridge began in 1912, according to another - a year later.If you believe some sources, the completion date of the mega-construction is 1921, others claim that it is 1923. At least a report entitled "Construction of a Concrete Railway Viaduct in Ceylon" was published by the Ceylon Engineering Association in 1923.Most guidebooks, as a rule, attribute the construction of the bridge to the local Ceylonese builder P.K. Appukhami in “co-authorship” with some British engineers. In fact, there is a funny legend circulating regarding Comrade Appuhami and his role in the construction of the bridge. Evil tongues claim that he is not a builder.Allegedly in 1912, the popular drummer and performer of “devil dances” (yakṣa næṭuma) in Ceylon P.K. Appuhami was returning with another panty in the lift of that same Devil-Yaksha (Yakṣayā). At the station in Ohiya, he came across a certain son of Foggy Albion, who almost “did not move his horses” from fright, seeing the Yaksha appearance of our Phil Collins, Dave Grohl and Cozy Powell of the Sri Lankan “spill” in “one bottle”. Thank God, the Briton did not “grunt” and through him Appuhami ended things with the bridge builders and, as some not very trustworthy sources say, received the unofficial status of the chief engineer of the project. Whether this is true or not - only the drummer himself knows...The chief designer and manager of the “Railway Line to Ceylon” project was D.J. Vimalasurendra, supposedly another eminent Ceylonese engineer and inventor. The designer of the viaduct is said to be Harold Cuthbert Marwood of the Railway Construction Department of the Ceylon State Railway. And another epic Aboriginal tale associated with the personality of P.K. Appuhami: British engineers, led by the mentioned Mr. Marwood, have completely broken their heads, excuse the tautology - how to install 9 columns in the swampy quagmire of a valley? And then again - and like a jack-in-the-box, that same Appukhami!!!Ceylon drummer proposed an ingenious move, like “cowards worth a ruble or forty,”: throwing huge boulders into the depression until they fill it. And on this “piled foundation” the columns were then installed!!! The huge bridge is located at an altitude of 945 meters above sea level, which is why its second name is “Bridge in the Sky”. By the way, the uniqueness of this railway bridge beauty lies in the fact that it is entirely built from rocks, bricks and cement - without the use of steel or iron!!!And again, another story: when construction work began, the First World War broke out almost immediately. And, quite expectedly, the front needed iron... It seems that everything is clear: no material - no bridge!!! But the skillful Ceylonese peasants took and built the Bridge from bricks, cobblestones and cement. Without iron, therefore... How long can you do it skillfully? And now - from the realm of mysteries and mysticism... When I saw the Nine Arches Bridge, I was struck by the feeling of that same déjà vu: I have already seen this building!!! Well, or something very, very similar!!!Of course: Istanbul's Bozdogan, Tarragona's "Devil's Bridge", Rome's Parco degli Acquedotti... And what do we get? Dear Sri Lankan bridge builders, I suppose, who had no idea about antiquity, simply erected a unique arched bridge in the style of ancient Roman viaducts without any iron load-bearing elements, using only stone, brick and cement??? A masterpiece of bridge construction based on technology a couple of millennia old??? Do you believe this yourself, my dear reader???Go ahead. Surely you noticed the unique bricks from which the bridge was built. The surface of the bricks is not flat, but convex (external lining) or concave (internal lining). So: neither the then Ceylon nor the metropolis (that is, Britain) knew the technology for making such figured and, as it turned out, durable bricks. And you, like the author of these lines, will probably not find information about where this brick was made. But this is not ten, not a hundred, or even a thousand pieces of figured brick - it had to be made somewhere???Next - the very same - and again I use this word - UNIQUE - concrete: eternal, which resembles antique, the secret of which scientists have not yet unraveled (this concrete only becomes stronger over time, unlike modern concrete). More riddles? Yes, easily - I have them!!! Have you noticed the “smoky” appearance of the structure? It was so blackened already about 80 years ago - look at the photo from the middle of the last century!!! But how and why did “Bridge to Heaven” become so terribly “smoky” in such a short period of time???One more thing: after the discovery of photography in 1822 by the French inventor Joseph Nicéphore Niepce, the topic of capturing everything and everyone quickly spread throughout the world. And the British, with their usual scrupulousness, began to photograph those same “everything and everything,” especially focusing on some significant events (including in the dominions and colonies). So - it turned out to be impossible to find ANY photographs of the construction of this grandiose facility for Ceylon!!! I don’t want to seem suspicious, but don’t you think that the Nine Arches Bridge was built, after all, not on the officially announced dates (the beginning of the 20th century) and not by British-Lankan builders, as the official history says???This, I am not afraid of this word, artifact in its mystery is very reminiscent of the carved columns of the temple in the Indian city of Shravanabelagola, the Inca polygonal masonry in Peruvian Ollantaytambo, the dolmens of the Western Caucasus, stone balls at the mouth of the Costa Rican Diquis River, the Newgrange mound in Ireland, the White Pyramid in Chinese province of Shaanxi, Skara Brae complex on the shores of the Scottish Bay of Skyll etc. That is, those very objects whose origin modern science is unable to explain... As a version: for the railway “Bridge to the Sky” in Sri Lanka, they simply took and adapted an already existing ANTIQUE VIADUCT!!!I answer the question in the air - why was the construction of the bridge attributed to the Sri Lankans (plus the “co-authors”, the British)? When there is no explanation for how an ancient Roman viaduct appeared on an island in the Indian Ocean, it occurred to someone “wise” to simply invent and fit the inexplicable fact described above into the official version. By the way, the Bridge of Nine Arches has NEVER been restored - it has retained its original charm and is still functioning. Isn't this a miracle??? Or just another mystery of an ancient civilization (by the way, maybe even an alien one). Highly recommend!!!

body: Eighteen of us, travelling together with Flamingo Tours, visited the Nine Arch bridge on 10th September 2023. After visiting Demodera Railway Station, we hired tuk-tuks up to the bridge site - about five kilometres as the approach is not motorable by car.This railway bridge, constructed in 1921, entirely of stone bricks and cement, lies between Ella and Demodera railway stations. It joins two hills along the rail line and is 80 - 100 feet high and 300 feet long.The bridge itself, bathed in morning sunlight, was a breathtaking sight at both ends. We walked along the rail line, atop the bridge to the far side and back. On either side of the bridge are little kiosks that sell king coconuts and other fruits.We were amongst a large crowd of tourists awaiting the arrival of the train. Seeing the approaching train on this concave shaped nine arch bridge was certainly a memorable and a wonderful sight. body: I wish Lonely Planet has covered this more thoroughly. Hope whoever reading this will find the following tips helpful:1) If you take the entrance near 98 Acres, the entrance has a mini colorful Hindu shrine and a coconut stand. Follow the signs and walk uphill until you reach a fork with no sign in the middle of the hill, take the left fork that will bring you through a muddy path and keeps walking for another five min or so before you can see the bridge below you on the far left. Both my partner and I were in sneakers and we were slipping and almost fell on a few occasions when we tried to climb down the slope. Many people also found it challenging towards the end.I am a 5 feet 2 Asian who rarely exercised. I managed to get down in one piece using an umbrella as a hiking stick and towards the end I had to rely on my hand on the ground to keep myself from slipping a few times. I also had help from my partner and a few kind tourists. I would feel a lot safer with trekking shoes and a hiking stick, and I would not recommend visiting this place if it is raining. 3) Try to ask your hotel for the train schedule. The experience was so much more fun with the train passing by with passengers waving and cheering. A few brave tourists sat on the bridge when the train passed by. body: My wife, our grandson Ryan and I, left our car at Ella Railway Station on 23rd July 2019 and hired a tuk-tuk to see the Nine Arch Bridge. The road to the bridge is in bad state of disrepair and narrow with sharp curves. Although we hired a tuk-tuk, one can walk from the Ella station, along the railway line, to the Nine Arch Bridge, a distance of about 3 kilometers. There are only a few trains plying this route. The tuk-tuk driver hurried along to be in time to show us the train crossing over the bridge. The bridge, as the name suggests, is built over nine arches atop tall walls, and runs over the 100 ft deep ravine. It is called the "sky bridge" emphasising the depth of the ravine. On that beautiful sunny morning, it was a wonderful sight to observe the train moving over this unique bridge. The train moved slowly over the bridge allowing me to capture a few attractive photographs. The bridge had been commissioned in 1921, built during the British Rule. The world war I broke out while it was being built. The consignment of steel earmarked for the bridge was diverted to the army for projects associated with the war. If steel were available, the bridge could have been built with only two or three spans across the ravine. Since there was no steel available, the engineers incorporated eight shorter spans supporting the bridge over these nine convex arches. Blocks of stone joined together with cement were the sole construction materials used in its construction. On its journey from Ella to Demodera the railway line passes through a 60 metre long tunnel about 75 metres after the arch bridge. Don’t miss out on taking a photo with you at the entrance to the tunnel! There were many excited tourists watching the train moving along!! The tuk-tuk driver Rathnayake (QP8422) dropped us at Demodera Railway Station for our train ride back to Ella after seeing the famed Demodera Loop.

title: Enjoyable trek with a rewarding end

body: Set in a deep valley the path down is prettty steep in places (not wheelchair / buggy friendly), but worth the walk and scramble at the end. Small cafe for drinks. Lush vegetation all the way down. Wasn't crowded on the day we went at end of April, managed to video the 12:45 train coming over the viaduct. Built by the British as part of their legacy of infrastructure, it looks well maintained and the line is in full use. We spotteda hornets nest hanging underneath (also can be seen on some tress). You get full access to track and its free - no barbed wire fences and prison threats if you stray near the track. Everybody just steps back as the train comes through and into a short tunnel at the end of the bridge.

body: We took a tuk tuk to the top of the goat track leading down to the bridge. With teenagers looking for some adventure this provided it in spades. The driver raced and gave the kids some fun. The walk down was a bit tough after some rain. It is a goat track and slippery. It’s always easier climbing up, so the return was better. The views and photo opportunities were fantastic. The bridge is amazing with a fair number of tourists snapping away to post on social media. Don’t you love the poses!I walked into the tunnel but got spooked thinking about if a train came, though there is room.I just love old stuff and this bridge and the rail tracks fitted the bill. The icing on the cake was the beautiful surroundings. It’s gorgeous.The next day we took the train from Ella to Demodara across the bridge which was also a great experience. I recommend this. It takes 15 minutes or so and at 10 rupees a bargain.Our kids loved this whole part of our holiday.
